 3.11 Centripetal Force.

 According to Newton's first law of motion, whenever a body moves in a straight line with uniform
velocity, no force is required to maintain this velocity. But when a body moves along a circular path with
uniform speed, its direction changes continuously i.e. velocity keeps on changing on account of a change

in direction. According to Newton's second law of motion, a change in the direction of motion of the body
can take place only if some external force acts on the body.
 Due to inertia, at every point of the circular path; the body tends to move along the tangent to the
circular path at that point (in figure). Since every body has directional inertia, a
velocity cannot change by itself and as such we have to apply a force. But this v
 v
force should be such that it changes the direction of velocity and not its
magnitude. This is possible only if the force acts perpendicular to the direction F
 F F
of velocity. Because the velocity is along the tangent, this force must be along F
the radius (because the radius of a circle at any point is perpendicular to the
tangent at that point). Further, as this force is to move the body in a circular v
 v
path, it must acts towards the centre. This centre-seeking force is called the
centripetal force.
 Hence, centripetal force is that force which is required to move a body in a circular path with uniform
speed. The force acts on the body along the radius and towards centre.

 Projection from a moving Platform:-
 Case (1) : When a ball is thrown upward from a truck moving with an uniform
 speed, then observer A standing in the truck, will see the ball moving in
 straight vertical line (upward & downward). The observer B sitting on road
 will see the ball moving in a parabolic path. The horizontal speed of the ball
 is equal to the speed of the truck.

 Case (2) : When a ball is thrown at some angle ‘ ’ in the direction of motion
 of the truck horizontal & vertical component of ball’s velocity w.r.t. observer
 A standing on the truck is u cos  and u sin  respectively. Horizontal &
 vertical component of ball’s velocity w.r.t. observer B sitting on the ground is
 ux = ucos  + v and u y = usin  respectively.

 Case (3) : When a ball is thrown at some angle ‘ ’ in the opposite direction
 of motion of the truck horizontal & vertical component of ball’s velocity
 w.r.t. observer A standing on the truck is u cos  and u sin  respectively.
 Horizontal & vertical component of ball’s velocity w.r.t. observer B sitting on
 the ground is u x = ucos  – v and u y = usin  respectively.

 2.1 Position.
 Any object is situated at point O and three observers from three different places are looking for same
object, then all three observers will have different observations about the position of point O and no one
will be wrong. Because they are observing the object from their different positions.
 Observer ‘A’ says : Point O is 3 m away in west W N O
direction. E

 Therefore position of any point is completely
expressed by two factors: Its distance from the observer and its direction with respect to observer.
 That is why position is characterised by a vector known as position vector.

 2.2 Rest and Motion.
 If a body does not change its position as time passes with respect to frame of reference, it is said to
be at rest.
And if a body changes its position as time passes with respect to frame of reference, it is said to be in
motion.
Frame of Reference : It is a system to which a set of coordinates are attached and with reference to which
observer describes any event.
 A passenger standing on platform observes that tree on a platform is at rest. But when the same
passenger is passing away in a train through station, observes that tree is in motion. In both conditions
observer is right. But observations are different because in first situation observer stands on a platform,
which is reference frame at rest and in second situation observer moving in train, which is reference frame
in motion.
 So rest and motion are relative terms. It depends upon the frame of references.

 Motion of freely falling body. Motion of billiards ball. Motion of flying insect.

 2.4 Particle or Point Mass.
 The smallest part of matter with zero dimension which can be described by its mass and position is
defined as a particle.
 If the size of a body is negligible in comparison to its range of motion then that body is known as a
particle.
 A body (Group of particles) to be known as a particle depends upon types of motion. For example in a
planetary motion around the sun the different planets can be presumed to be the particles.
 In above consideration when we treat body as particle, all parts of the body undergo same
displacement and have same velocity and acceleration.

Motion in Two Dimension

 The motion of an object is called two dimensional, if two of the three co-ordinates are
required to specify the position of the object in space changes w.r.t time.
 In such a motion, the object moves in a plane. For example, a billiard ball moving over the
billiard table, an insect crawling over the floor of a room, earth revolving around the sun etc.
 Two special cases of motion in two dimension are 1. Projectile motion 2. Circular
motion

 PROJECTILE MOTION

 3.1 Introduction.
 A hunter aims his gun and fires a bullet directly towards a monkey sitting on a distant tree. If the
monkey remains in his position, he will be safe but at the instant the bullet leaves the barrel of gun, if the
monkey drops from the tree, the bullet will hit the monkey because the bullet will not follow the linear path.

 The path of motion of a bullet will be parabolic and this motion of bullet is defined as projectile motion.
 If the force acting on a particle is oblique with initial velocity then the motion of particle is called projectile
motion.
 3.2 Projectile.
 A body which is in flight through the atmosphere but is not being propelled by any fuel is called
projectile.
Example: (i) A bomb released from an aeroplane in level flight

 (ii) A bullet fired from a gun

 (iii) An arrow released from bow

 (iv) A Javelin thrown by an athlete

3.3 Assumptions of Projectile Motion.

 (1) There is no resistance due to air.

 (2) The effect due to curvature of earth is negligible.

 (3) The effect due to rotation of earth is negligible.
 (4) For all points of the trajectory, the acceleration due to gravity ‘g’ is constant in magnitude and
direction.
 3.4 Principles of Physical Independence of Motions.

 (1) The motion of a projectile is a two-dimensional motion. So, it can be discussed in two parts.
Horizontal motion and vertical motion. These two motions take place independent of each other. This is
called the principle of physical independence of motions.

 (2) The velocity of the particle can be resolved into two mutually perpendicular components.
Horizontal component and vertical component.

 (3) The horizontal component remains unchanged throughout the flight. The force of gravity
continuously affects the vertical component.

 (4) The horizontal motion is a uniform motion and the vertical motion is a uniformly accelerated retarded
motion.
 3.5 Types of Projectile Motion.

 (1) Oblique projectile motion (2) Horizontal projectile motion (3) Projectile motion on an inclined
plane

SECTIONS 02-03
Projectile Motion: Meaning and Types

Begin with the definition, assumptions and the two common launch situations.

 02 WHAT IS PROJECTILE MOTION

 Scientific definition
 When a particle is projected into the air and, after projection, the only force acting on it is gravitational force,
 neglecting air resistance, its motion is called projectile motion.

Projectile motion normally means two-dimensional motion under gravity. It has simultaneous horizontal and vertical
components. A simple vertical upward throw is one-dimensional motion and should not be used as the general definition.

 Air resistance is neglected.
 Gravity is uniform and acts vertically downward. AFTER PROJECTION - UPWARD-POSITIVE AXES

 The particle is treated as a point mass. aₓ = 0 aᵧ = -g
 Earth’s curvature and rotation are neglected over the x horizontal; y upward
 motion.

 03 TYPES

 HORIZONTAL OBLIQUE

 u at θ

 uᵧ = 0 uₓ = u cos θ

 Focus of this module
 Detailed derivations in the following sections use HORIZONTAL PROJECTILE MOTION: initial velocity is horizontal and
 initial vertical velocity is zero.

Force and Acceleration

 04 FORCE AND ACCELERATION

 FREE-BODY DIAGRAM

 HORIZONTAL ACCELERATION
 aₓ = 0
 particle No horizontal force

 VERTICAL ACCELERATION - UPWARD POSITIVE
 aᵧ = -g

 Gravity acts downward
 Weight = mg

 Why does horizontal velocity remain constant?
 Newton’s second law gives aₓ = Fₓ/m = 0. Therefore vₓ does
 Only force after projection not change. Gravity supplies a constant vertical acceleration,
 so vᵧ changes continuously with time.

 TWO MOTIONS, ONE TRAJECTORY

 HORIZONTAL MOTION VERTICAL MOTION

 Uniform motion Uniformly accelerated

 vₓ = constant; aₓ = 0 vᵧ changes; aᵧ = -g

 Core idea
 The two motions share the same time t, but their equations are applied independently. Combining their positions
 produces the curved path.

Basic Equations

For the derivations, take +x horizontally and downward vertical displacement y as positive.

 06 SIGN CONVENTION AND EQUATIONS

 Chosen sign convention
 Origin at the launch point. Positive x is horizontal in the launch direction. Positive y is vertically downward. Therefore the
 vertical acceleration is +g in these equations.

HORIZONTAL DIRECTION VERTICAL DIRECTION

 x = ut y = ½gt²

 VELOCITY VELOCITY
 vₓ = u vᵧ = gt

 ACCELERATION ACCELERATION
 aₓ = 0 aᵧ = g

 If you choose upward-positive y
 Then aᵧ = -g and the vertical coordinate measured from the launch point is y = -½gt². The physics is identical. Never mix
 equations from two sign conventions in one solution.

 ONE CLOCK LINKS BOTH DIRECTIONS

 At any instant t, use the same time in x = ut and y = ½gt².

SECTION 07
Derivation: Time of Flight

Time of flight is the time from launch until the particle reaches the ground.

 07 TIME OF FLIGHT

 Vertical displacement at landing
 1 y = h

 Use vertical equation
 2 h = ½gt²

 Multiply by 2
 3 2h = gt²

 Divide by g
 4 t² = 2h/g

 Take the positive root
 5 t = √(2h/g)

 TIME OF FLIGHT
 t = √(2h/g)

 Choose the positive root because time after launch is positive

 Important conceptual result
 Time of flight depends on height h and gravity g. It does NOT depend on horizontal velocity u. Two particles launched
 horizontally at different speeds from the same height land at the same time, if air resistance is neglected.

 Increase h → longer flight Increase g → shorter flight Change u → flight time unchanged

Horizontal range R is the horizontal distance travelled before reaching the ground.

 09 HORIZONTAL RANGE

 Horizontal equation

 At the landing point

 Use the time of flight
 3 t = √(2h/g)

 Substitute
 4 R = u√(2h/g)

 HORIZONTAL RANGE
 R = u√(2h/g)

 valid for horizontal projection from height h

HOW THE RANGE RESPONDS

 Change Effect on R Reason

 Increase u R increases directly R u for fixed h and g

 Increase h R increases as √h More time is available to move horizontally

 Increase g R decreases as 1/√g The particle falls faster

 Scaling insight
 Doubling u doubles R. Doubling h multiplies R by √2, not by 2. Quadrupling h doubles R.

Velocity Components

The direction of motion changes because only the vertical component grows.

 v vᵧ = gt

 RESULTANT SPEED
 v = √(u² + g²t²)

 from Pythagoras

 At launch
 t = 0, so vᵧ = 0 and the velocity is exactly horizontal.

 During flight
 vₓ remains constant. vᵧ increases downward by g every second. The resultant velocity therefore becomes steeper and its
 magnitude increases.

 Direction angle
 If φ is measured below the horizontal, tan φ = vᵧ/vₓ = gt/u. This relation describes how the velocity vector rotates downward.

 Velocity changes in direction and magnitude - even though vₓ stays constant.

SECTION 12
Solved Numerical Problems 1-2

Follow the same structure every time: Given → Required → Formula → Substitute → Calculate → Answer.

 12 SOLVED PROBLEMS

 1 Default simulator problem

 GIVEN u = 2 m/s, h = 10 m, g = 9.8 m/s²

 REQUIRED Time of flight t and horizontal range R

 FORMULA t = √(2h/g); R = ut

 SUBSTITUTION t = √(20/9.8); R = 2t

 CALCULATION t = √2.0408 = 1.4286 s; R = 2 × 1.4286 = 2.8572 m

 FINAL ANSWER t ≈ 1.43 s; R ≈ 2.86 m

 The fall time comes from vertical motion; the range is horizontal speed multiplied by that time.

 2 Faster launch from a taller cliff

 GIVEN u = 8 m/s, h = 20 m, g = 10 m/s²

 REQUIRED Time of flight t and range R

 FORMULA t = √(2h/g); R = ut

 SUBSTITUTION t = √(40/10); R = 8t

 CALCULATION t = √4 = 2 s; R = 8 × 2 = 16 m

 FINAL ANSWER t = 2.00 s; R = 16.0 m

 The chosen values make the square root exact. A larger u affects range but not the 2 s fall time.

Solved Numerical Problem 5

Use scaling to predict a change before performing the full calculation.

 5 Effect of increasing launch height

 GIVEN u = 6 m/s, g = 10 m/s²; h1 = 20 m, h2 = 80 m

 REQUIRED Compare t and R

 FORMULA t = √(2h/g); R = ut

 SUBSTITUTION t1 = √(40/10) = 2 s; t2 = √(160/10) = 4 s

 CALCULATION R1 = 6 × 2 = 12 m; R2 = 6 × 4 = 24 m

 FINAL ANSWER t doubles: 2 s → 4 s; R doubles: 12 m → 24 m

 Height becomes four times larger. Because t and R vary as √h, each becomes twice as large.

Quick Revision Sheet

 17 REVISION

 Definition

 Two-dimensional motion after projection when gravity is the only force, with air resistance neglected.

DOWNWARD-POSITIVE FROM THE LAUNCH POINT

 HORIZONTAL POSITION VERTICAL DISPLACEMENT
 x = ut y = ½gt²

 TIME OF FLIGHT HORIZONTAL RANGE
 t = √(2h/g) R = u√(2h/g)

 VELOCITY COMPONENTS RESULTANT SPEED
 vₓ = u, vᵧ = gt v = √(u² + g²t²)

 TRAJECTORY ACCELERATION
 y = gx²/(2u²) aₓ = 0, aᵧ = g ↓

 REMEMBER THIS

 Horizontal and vertical motions use the same time.
 Find time from vertical motion, then find range horizontally.
 t is independent of u; R is directly proportional to u.
 A sign change from coordinate choice does not change the physics.

 Units: u, v in m/s • h, x, y, R in m • t in s • g in m/s²
